- speckit-converge: Assess the current codebase against the feature's spec, plan, and tasks, then append any remaining unbuilt work as new tasks to tasks.md so implement can complete it.

- speckit-plan: Execute the implementation planning workflow using the plan template to generate design artifacts.
- speckit-specify: Create or update the feature specification from a natural language feature description.
- speckit-tasks: Generate an actionable, dependency-ordered tasks.md for the feature based on available design artifacts.
- speckit-taskstoissues: Convert existing tasks into actionable, dependency-ordered GitHub issues for the feature based on available design artifacts.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them.   that a caller cannot reach it alone. **A session with it switched off is bounded
  by nothing time-based at all**, and the four constraints around this one are
  then the whole of the containment. That is a state an operator may choose; it is
  not a state anything here prevents.

  *Amended 2.0.0: an idle timeout was required here until 2026-08-14. It was
  withdrawn because it bounded the wrong thing — a session waiting for a human is
  quiet, and destroying it for that lost work the operator expected to keep — not
  because it was mis-measured. What it cost to remove is written above.*
- Teardown is **verified**, not assumed. An orphaned tmux window is a live
  unsandboxed shell with no owner.
- The listener binds **loopback only**. Reachability comes from the tunnel.

A feature that widens any of these needs an explicit justification in the plan
naming what now becomes reachable.

### VII. Design system is binding

[`docs/design-system.md`](../../docs/design-system.md) and
[`docs/components.md`](../../docs/components.md) define the vocabulary for the
dashboard.

- Tokens only — never a hard-coded colour, size, or font in a template.
- Reuse the canonical component. A second session card is a defect.
- **Pane output is rendered as text, never as HTML.** Everything a Claude session
  prints reaches the browser. This is the project's only XSS surface and it is
  closed by construction, not by sanitising.

---

## Development Workflow

Three lanes, one set of rules. All inherit these principles.

| Lane | When | Path |
|---|---|---|
| **Feature** | More than one moving part | constitution → `/speckit-specify` → `/speckit-plan` → `/speckit-tasks` → `/speckit-implement` |
| **Quick fix** | One-line bug, typo, copy | Fix → verify → one line in `docs/fixes-log.md` |
| **Automated** | Issue labelled `claude-fix` | Runner → bounded run → **PR only, never `main`** |

Autonomous execution (`ralph/loop.sh`) works the plan **one task per iteration**
with a fresh context each time, and commits after each. It is bound by every
principle above.

---

## Quality Gates

A change may merge only when all of these are true:

- [ ] Build, test, and lint green (the `AGENTS.md` commands)
- [ ] New behaviour has a test that fails without the change
- [ ] `docs/security.md` checklist satisfied for anything touching input, authz, or secrets
- [ ] `docs/auth-and-sessions.md` checklist satisfied, if auth or the session lifecycle was touched
- [ ] Cross-session isolation still holds; teardown still verified
- [ ] `docs/design-system.md` + `docs/components.md` respected for anything visual
- [ ] No `NEEDS CLARIFICATION` left unanswered
- [ ] Reviewed by a code owner (`.github/CODEOWNERS`)

---

## Governance

This constitution supersedes all other practice. Amending it requires a pull
request that states what changed, why, and what it breaks — reviewed by a code
owner like any other change.

Complexity must be justified in the plan. "It might be useful later" is not a
justification.

Agents: `AGENTS.md` is your runtime guide; this document is the authority behind it.

# Go Conventions

> Loaded when: writing or changing any Go in this repo.
> `AGENTS.md` states these rules; this file shows them.

## Naming

Standard Go. Packages lowercase and singular; no `util`, no `common` — a package
named for what it contains rather than what it does becomes a drawer.

```go
package session       // files: manager.go, manager_test.go
func (m *Manager) Create(ctx context.Context, req CreateRequest) (*Session, error)
```

## Errors

Never swallow one. Wrap with `%w` and context; return, do not log-and-continue.

```go
if err := m.tmux.Kill(ctx, s.Target()); err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("kill session %s: %w", s.ID, err)  // never a bare `return err`
}
```

Sentinel errors for conditions a caller branches on (`ErrSessionNotFound`), checked
with `errors.Is` rather than by string.

**Never put a secret, a prompt, or pane content in an error string.** Errors travel
to logs, and `docs/security.md` §3 makes all three secret. A bare `return err` from a
package that touched the host is how tmux's own stderr ends up in the audit trail.

## Tests

Table-driven, `t.Parallel()`, no network, no real tmux — `tmuxctl.Controller` is an
interface with a fake, and the fake records exact argv so a test can assert no shell
string was ever built.

Every PR needs a test that fails without the change. Auth and session code also needs
the **negative** cases: bad signature, stale timestamp, replay, wrong owner.

```go
req := signedRequest(t, a, `{"cwd":"/repo"}`)
mustVerify(t, a, req)                            // first use passes
if _, err := a.Verify(clone(t, req)); err == nil {
    t.Fatal("replayed request was accepted")     // this is the whole point
}
```

Tests that need a real tmux or a real binary live behind a build tag — `//go:build
tmux` for the integration suite, `//go:build quickstart` for an acceptance run — so
that `go test ./...` stays fast and hermetic. Both are in the command table in
`AGENTS.md`; neither runs by default.

**A test that cannot fail is not a test.** Three defects in this repo shipped with
full green suites. Two because the thing under test had no production caller: the
reaper, and the idle clock. The third because the fake agreed with the daemon
about a field neither of them carried — the session lifetime was written to no
tmux option and read back from none, and every adoption test passed while a
never-expiring session came back mortal. Assert the caller, not only the callee,
and make the fake hold what the host holds.

## Comments

Explain *why*, never *what*. If the code needs a "what" comment, rewrite the code.

The comments worth writing are the ones that stop a later reader "fixing" something
correct. This repo has several — `path` vs `PATH` in a zsh function, `=name` vs
`=name:` for a tmux target, `alg` read only to reject — and each exists because
somebody lost time to it once.

579	
580	`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/crswd/sessions-.jsonl`, else `~/.config/crswd/sessions-.jsonl`.
581	It is the only durable state the daemon keeps, and it exists because the host
582	stopped being sufficient: on 2026-08-22 the kernel OOM killer took a whole
583	`tmux-spawn` cgroup and destroyed a session's tmux state along with it, so
584	everything recorded on that tmux session went too.
585	
586	**What it holds**: session id, owner, session name, conversation identifier,
587	working directory, start-command *name*, lifetime, original creation time, and a
588	revival attempt count. That is the set the daemon cannot rediscover once the
589	shell is gone. The session name is caller-supplied but not free text:
590	`ValidateName` holds it to `^[a-zA-Z0-9-]{1,64}$` before it is a session's, and a
591	revival cannot render its start command without it.
592	
593	**What it must never hold**: a bearer token, a token hash, pane content,
594	conversation content, or caller-supplied free text. The rule FR-042 places on the
595	audit trail applies here unchanged — there is simply no request behind this file.
596	A start-command *name* is recorded and a command *line* never is: a stored
597	command line would be a command line a restart could be made to run.
598	
599	**Mode `0600`**, created with the directory at `0700`.
600	
601	**One journal per daemon, named after its listen address** — the same thing the
602	tmux server is named after (`tmuxctl.SocketFor`). Two daemons on one host must not
603	replay each other's sessions any more than they may see each other's shells, and
604	without this they do: a second daemon sharing a home directory replays the first
605	one's journal, finds those sessions absent from its *own* tmux server, and stands
606	ready to recreate every one of them on it.
607	
608	**Append-only, fsynced per record.** The failure being defended against is an
609	unclean stop, and a rewritten document degrades to a truncated file where a log
610	degrades to a missing last line. On this host the unclean reset of 2026-08-17
611	lost a flag out of a rewritten `~/.claude.json` and took a gitignored `.env` with
612	it — that is the failure mode, observed, on this machine.
613	
614	**Reading it is fail-loud, replaying it is fail-safe.** A missing file means no
615	session has been created yet. An unreadable one is fatal at startup, because a
616	daemon that continued would supervise nothing and report nothing. A torn final
617	line is discarded and counted. And every replayed candidate is re-checked against
618	the allowlist, the ceiling and the cap in force *now* — a journal outlives the
619	configuration that produced it, and it must never reinstate a session the
620	operator's current configuration would refuse to create.

662	FR-025 says a transcript is never opened, because Claude's file name is the id and its
663	directory is the working directory. Codex keys rollouts by date and the working directory
664	exists only inside line 1, so listing a Codex directory's conversations opens each rollout
665	**once, bounded**: at most 64 KiB read, stopping at the first newline, decoding only `type`,
666	`payload.id` and `payload.cwd`. Nothing it reads is rendered or logged. It scans at most 500
667	rollout files, newest date directory first, and returns at most 50 matches. Claude's listing
668	still opens nothing.
669	
670	### Codex's update check (spec 019 D5)
671	
672	Codex checks for a new release on startup and offers to install it. A line typed into a pane
673	can answer that offer, so an update prompt is a way for typed input to install software. The
674	daemon therefore adds `-c check_for_update_on_startup=false` to every Codex line it types
675	(and `--no-alt-screen`, without which tmux keeps no scrollback), and configuration refuses a
676	Codex command that sets the check back to true. It is a daemon-owned flag, not an operator
677	choice, because a forgotten flag costs a global package install.
678	
679	### Codex's dangerous flags are the operator's
680	
681	`--dangerously-skip-permissions` is the operator's choice for Claude Code, and for Codex the
682	equivalents are `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` (no approval prompts, no sandbox)
683	and `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` (hooks run without review). The daemon adds neither.
684	Put them in the `codex` entry of `start_commands` if you want unattended sessions, with the
685	same consequences as for Claude: a request that passes auth runs code on this host unsandboxed.
686	
687	## Rate limiting & audit
688	
689	- Per-caller rate limit on session creation. Spawning Claude sessions is expensive
690	  and unbounded spawning is a local denial of service. **Both doors create**, so the
691	  browser's create calls the same limiter and the same validation rather than a second
692	  copy of either.
693	- Per-source rate limit on `POST /login`, on **the same token bucket**, which is generic
694	  over its key rather than duplicated: a create's budget is spent by an identity because
695	  it sits behind layer 2, and a sign-in's is spent by an address because establishing an
696	  identity is what it is for. The type parameter is what keeps one from being spent by
697	  the other's key. Two limiters over two copies of the bucket would be two rules about
698	  what a budget is, free to disagree.
699	- **What that limiter remembers is bounded by its own sweep**, and since the sign-in
700	  budget exists that is load-bearing: its keys are addresses a stranger chooses, so what
701	  keeps the map small is that every decision drops every bucket that has refilled to the
702	  top — an entry survives only while it is partly spent.
703	- Cap concurrent sessions; refuse past the cap rather than degrading the host.
704	- **Every request is audited**: timestamp, caller ID, action, session ID, decision.
705	  Audit records carry no prompt text and no session output.
706	- A browser action is audited under its own name — `dashboard.create`,
707	  `dashboard.destroy`, `dashboard.rename`, `dashboard.compact` — and a request the
708	  action gate refused under `dashboard.reject`, deliberately not `access.reject`: an
709	  identity that got in and *then* failed the cross-site check is a different and more
710	  alarming event than one that never got in, and an operator counting one must not be
711	  counting the other with it.
712	- **What was delivered is never recorded.** The compact's own text is a constant the
713	  daemon sends into a session; the record says the action happened, never its content.
714	  Every reason on the trail is a sentinel this codebase authored, so a record can
715	  never carry a byte the caller chose.
716	
717	## Pre-merge security checklist
718	
719	- [ ] No secret added to the repo (CI + push protection verify this)
720	- [ ] Every new endpoint enforces authn **and** ownership server-side
721	- [ ] Session IDs unguessable; a session another caller owns, or one that never
722	      existed, returns 404 and not 403 — the 403 is the action gate's answer to a
723	      request it would not accept at all, and the two never stand in for each other
724	- [ ] Any new mutating browser route goes through the action gate, not just layer 1,
725	      and both halves of that gate are tested with the other satisfied
726	- [ ] Input decoded into a typed struct with unknown fields rejected
727	- [ ] No shell string built; `exec.Command` with argv only
728	- [ ] Any caller-supplied path allowlisted and symlink-resolved
729	- [ ] Auth failures are uniform and leak no detail about which check failed
730	- [ ] No session output, prompt, or token in any log line
731	- [ ] Listener still bound to loopback, or bound wider only on a daemon whose
732	      layer 1 admits somebody
733	- [ ] A new setting a secret could be written into is classified by `config.IsSecret`,
734	      so the 0600 refusal and the settings page cannot disagree about it
735	- [ ] No secret value on any rendered page — swept across every route, not reasoned about
736	- [ ] No new dependency without justification, and the root `go.sum` still absent
737	- [ ] No `Access-Control-Allow-*` on any route, either door — swept, not assumed
738	- [ ] Browser-door responses all carry the header set above, refusals included

That build says so instead, in as many words. The sentence names no value: the password's row is still `present` or `absent` and nothing else. ### The password door It authenticates *less* than Access does, and the difference is stated rather than smoothed over. Access verifies a person against an identity provider at the edge, before this host is reachable. The password door verifies that whoever is asking knows one secret — so there is one operator behind it by construction, no allowlist to check, and no edge failing closed in front of it. Everything behind the door is unchanged: the same `auth.CallerOperator`, the same ownership checks, the same action gate on anything that changes the host. - **The password is a secret by `config.IsSecret`**, so it is `present`/`absent` on the settings page and refused by `config.Editable`. A daemon whose file names a door the server did not build is a wiring defect, and a wiring defect must not be what puts a login form on the network; it is the same distinction the bind rule above draws. Every other path on the daemon — a page, an action, a path nothing claims — still meets the door. - **The password is read from the posted body and nowhere else.** Never the query string: a password this daemon would accept out of a URL is a password in a browser history, a referrer header, and every proxy log in between. - **The action gate is deliberately absent, and cannot apply.** Two of its three checks are the layer-1 identity and a page token bound to it, and neither exists before this route runs; half a gate would be the second, differently-shaped authorisation path there is exactly one of on this door. Absent still admits, unlike on an action route: a script signing in sends no header, and what bounds a script is that it has a source address and therefore a budget. This is a check on the *initiator*; it authorises nobody, and it is here because the budget below is a thing that can be exhausted. Without it the cheapest way to empty the operator's guesses is a hostile page making the operator's own browser spend them, from the operator's own address — a lockout on the one route that can end a lockout. - **Every attempt is counted against the address it came from**, at six a minute with a burst of three, on the same token bucket the create route spends — the port dropped, because a browser opens a new one per connection and a budget per connection is no budget at all; `RemoteAddr` and never `X-Forwarded-For`, because a limiter keyed by a value the caller writes is one the caller opts out of. It is spent **before** the two sides are compared, so a correct password does not buy its way past a spent budget, and it is not what makes guessing this password hopeless — the sixteen-character minimum is. What it buys is that guessing is slow, loud, and cheap to refuse. - **The refusal is this door's uniform 401, not the create route's 429.** A caller that proved who it is may be told to slow down; one that has proved nothing is told nothing, so a brute-forcer cannot tell a refused guess from a guess nobody read and cannot pace their attempts by the answer. - **`GET /login` is deliberately not on that budget.** Serving the form costs this daemon what refusing an unauthenticated request costs it anywhere else on this door, none of which is limited either — while a budget a page load could spend is a budget an `` on a hostile page could empty, and what it would empty is the operator's own way back in. - **A sign-in leaves one audit record either way** — `login.view` for the form, `login.submit` for an attempt, allowed or denied, the ones the budget and the cross-site check refused included — carrying no password material, because every reason on it is a sentinel this codebase authored. Four of them refuse here and the caller can tell none of them apart, so the trail is the only place they are ever distinguished. #### The way back out `POST /logout` clears the cookie, and it is registered from the same question the two routes above are — so the door a browser can open and the door it can close appear and disappear together. Where Cloudflare Access is the door it is not registered and the settings page draws no control, because what that browser holds is the edge's own `CF_Authorization`, which this daemon does not read and must not pretend to end. - **It is behind layer 1 and through the action gate**, on `handleAction` like every other mutating browser route. A service-token assertion presented to the browser door is refused exactly as a stranger's is. Neither door is allowed to skip the daemon-side check. Both doors resolve to one owner by construction, so the ownership check below runs on every request through either. Never trust the request Every request is authenticated **and** authorized on the server, on every call. There is no client to trust — the Claude skill is just another HTTP caller, and anyone can write one. ```go // Every API handler starts this way. No exceptions, no "internal" routes. func (s *Server) handle(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { caller, err := s.auth.Verify(r) // signature + timestamp + replay check if err != nil { // Uniform response: never reveal which check failed. http.Error(w, "unauthorized", http.StatusUnauthorized) s.log.Warn("auth rejected", "remote", r.RemoteAddr, "reason", err) return } sess, err := s.sessions.Get(sessionIDFrom(r)) if err != nil || sess.Owner != caller.ID { // ownership, not just authn http.Error(w, "not found", http.StatusNotFound) // 404, not 403 — no enumeration return } ... } ``` That is the API door. The browser door asks the same two questions with the other door's credential — validate the assertion, then check ownership — and answers with the same uniform refusal. What changes is the credential, never the questions, and neither door has a route exempt from either. A browser route that **changes** something asks two more before either of them, and they are not about who the caller is. The browser's credential is an ambient cookie, so "the operator's identity was verified" and "the operator asked for this" are different facts; the second is what the action gate establishes. See [`docs/auth-and-sessions.md`](./auth-and-sessions.md) for the rule in full — the short version is layer 1, then `Sec-Fetch-Site` (**absent refuses here**), then a stateless page token bound to the verified identity, all before the handler runs and therefore before anything changes. Check **ownership**, not just authentication. "Is this caller authenticated?" is not the same question as "does this caller own session `a3f9`?" Session IDs must be unguessable (`crypto/rand`, ≥128 bits) and must never be sequential. ### 2. Validate every input at the boundary Decode into a typed struct with `DisallowUnknownFields`. Reject anything unexpected. ```go func decode[T any](r *http.Request) (T, error) { var v T dec := json.NewDecoder(io.LimitReader(r.Body, maxBodyBytes)) dec.DisallowUnknownFields() if err := dec.Decode(&v); err != nil { return v, fmt.Errorf("malformed body: %w", err) } return v, validate(v) // struct tags; every field constrained } ``` Specific to this daemon: - **Never build a shell string.** Use `exec.Command` with an argv slice. No `sh -c`, no `fmt.Sprintf` into a command line. - **Caller text reaches tmux only through `load-buffer` on stdin, then `paste-buffer`** (bracketed, `-p`, on the session page's route). Text holding a C0 control other than TAB or LF is refused, because inside a bracketed paste `ESC[201~` would end the paste. Treat prompt text as hostile bytes. - **`send-keys` receives daemon constants only.** The session page's key bar sends a symbolic name, and the daemon maps it through a closed table. - The daemon never types into a working session on its own initiative. The one exception is the session page's input panel (spec 018): text or a key the operator sent, delivered once, when they pressed it. It never types from a timer, a supervisor, a dialog detector or any path without an operator request behind it. - **Working directories are allowlisted**, resolved with `filepath.Clean` + `filepath.EvalSymlinks`, then checked to be under an approved root. A caller does not get to name an arbitrary path. - **A suggestion is never an authorisation.** The create form offers directories — the approved roots, the operator's own list, and discovered children — and the field still submits an ordinary string, so the handler cannot tell a chosen path from a typed one and does not try. Both meet the same resolution, the same refusal and the same audit record. A path may legitimately be offered and refused: the list is presentation, the roots are the control. - **Session names are `^[a-zA-Z0-9-]{1,64}$`.** They become tmux target strings; a name containing `:` or `.` addresses a different window. ### 3. Secret hygiene - Secrets come from the environment, from 1Password, or from the operator's configuration file. Never a source file in this repository. - `.env` is gitignored; `.env.example` and `config.example` document the *names* only. `config.example` ships with every setting commented out, which is also what keeps a copy of it from being a file that holds a secret. - **Which keys are secret is one predicate — `config.IsSecret`** — and it is `shared_secret`, `access_allowed_emails` and `dashboard_password`. The allowlist is not a credential, but it names *who* may reach a daemon that runs unsandboxed code on this host. The password is the browser door itself on a daemon with no Cloudflare in front of it, which is why the predicate's third caller matters as much as the first two: `config.Editable` is `!IsSecret`, so naming it there is what keeps it out of the form on the page it protects. A second list would let the 0600 refusal, the settings page and that form disagree about what a secret is, and the disagreement surfaces as a credential in a browser rather than as a failure. - **A configuration file that sets any of them is refused unless it is mode 0600.** The refusal fires on the file's *contents*, not on its name: refusing over the mode of a file holding nothing but `allowed_roots` would demand a change that protects nothing, and an operator who cannot act on a refusal learns to work around it. - **No refusal about the file ever names the value it refused over.** The file's path, the offending key, and the line number are the whole of what an error may carry. - **Session output is secret.** Captured pane content can contain anything on the host — keys, tokens, customer data. Never log it, never ship it to telemetry, never include it in an error message. - **A session never receives this daemon's environment**, and that rule is what makes the one above enforceable rather than aspirational. A session is `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions`; a credential in its environment is one `env` away from being pane content, and pane content on this product travels into model context and a transcript that leaves the host. So the environment is **composed, never inherited** — `config.SessionEnvironment` is the single definition, it is an allowlist rather than a denylist so that a new secret-bearing setting is excluded on the day it is added, and it consults `IsSecret` rather than restating which keys are secret. The operator may name extra variables to pass through; naming a secret or any `CRSW_` variable is a **startup failure**, because a warning about a credential is a credential that ships. Two mechanisms enforce it: `cmd.Env` at `internal/tmuxctl`'s single exec chokepoint, and a startup reconciliation of the tmux server's global environment — the server outlives the daemon, so without the second every host that ran an older build stays exposed for as long as its server lives. Neither can clean a session already running; that limit is documented for the operator rather than papered over. - Never log the shared secret, a bearer token, or a full signed body. - Rotate anything ever committed — assume it is public forever. - GitHub secret scanning + push protection are enabled on this repo. ### 4. Fail closed Any error in the auth path denies the request. A missing config value that would weaken auth is a **startup failure**, not a warning: ```go if cfg.SharedSecret == "" { return fmt.Errorf("CRSW_SHARED_SECRET is required; refusing to start") } ``` A daemon that starts with auth disabled is worse than one that does not start. The same rule decides the startup dependency probe, and it is why the two dependencies fail differently. **`tmux` missing is fatal** — without it there is nothing this daemon can do, so starting would defer the failure to the operator's first create rather than prevent it. **A start command's binary missing is a warning** — the daemon can still serve the dashboard, adopt what is already on the host, and say what is wrong, and refusing there would take away the one thing that could tell them. The probe reads the *configured* commands rather than a fixed `claude`, **installs nothing, and never runs what it found**. A daemon that installs software is a daemon that can be made to install software, and one that executed a probed binary to see whether it works would be running an operator's command line at startup with no session to run it in. It does run **one** thing, and the bounds on it are the whole of why that is allowed. A start command is resolved inside a tmux pane's login shell, so a probe asking only this process's `PATH` warns about commands that work — and a check that is wrong about a healthy host trains an operator to ignore it. So the probe asks the login shell what `PATH` it has: - **A constant script on stdin**, `printf '%s\n' "$PATH"`, and the binary is resolved against the answer in Go. The command name is never named to the shell: `sh -lc "command -v $binary"` resolves identically and is exactly the shell string rule 2 forbids, built out of a configured value. - **`exec.CommandContext(ctx, shell, "-l")`** — argv, no `sh -c`, and every element past the program is a literal in the source. - **At most once per start, and only after this daemon's own `PATH` has already failed** to resolve a command. A host where everything is present never runs the operator's profile at all. - **Bounded**: a 5s timeout and a 1s wait delay, so a profile that blocks costs a start five seconds rather than hanging it. - **A shell that cannot be asked is a note, not a claim.** The probe says what it checked and what it could not, and never that the command is absent. The trade this takes is real and named here rather than buried: the daemon now executes a file it does not own (`~/.profile`) at startup. It is taken because the alternative was a check that lies, and it is bounded by every line above. ### 5. Dependencies - Dependabot is enabled. Security updates merge promptly, not eventually. - A new dependency needs justification: what does it do that stdlib cannot? The HTTP server, HMAC, and JSON handling are all stdlib. Keep it that way. - **`go.sum` must not exist**, and that is asserted by a test in the default build rather than remembered. It is the reason the configuration file is `key = value` hand-parsed: YAML and TOML have no standard-library parser, neither is safe to hand-roll, and a dependency for either would create the file this rule forbids. - **The rule covers the host module**, the root `go.mod` that builds the VM daemon and every release. The cluster build is a second module in `k8s/` (spec 017, `k8s-20c-plan.md` §5, decided 9/26/26) that reaches the root's `internal/` through `replace ../` and may carry `k8s.io/client-go` for the exec, watch and leader-election code the standard library lacks; nothing under the root imports `k8s/`, so the root `go.sum` stays absent and the three tests that assert it are unchanged. ## Configuration, and the page that shows it The configuration file is a second **source** for the values the loader already validates, and deliberately not a second set of rules. Everything it supplies goes through exactly the loader an environment variable goes through, so no bound, default or refusal is written twice and a value cannot mean one thing in a unit and another in a file. **Precedence is flag → environment → file → default**, decided in one shim. The order is the security property: reversed, a stale file on a host silently overrides the environment a container was configured with. A daemon with no file therefore behaves exactly as one built before the file existed, which is what makes the change safe to deploy at all. **Nothing in the daemon writes the operator's file.** `crswd config migrate` is the only code in this repository that writes a configuration file, and it is a command the operator runs. `GET /settings` renders that resolved configuration, and it is the one page holding every secret at render time: - **A secret's value is `present` or `absent` and nothing else.** Not a length, not a prefix, not a suffix, not a hash. A masked value is still a disclosure, and the four characters of a credential a page is willing to print are four an attacker no longer has to guess. The word is chosen in Go by `config.IsSecret` and reaches the template already decided, so there is no raw value beside it for a later render to reach for. - **The source column is recorded, never inferred.** The shim writes it as it decides. A file and an environment holding the same bytes are indistinguishable by comparison, and that is exactly the case an operator is on the page to ask about. - **No mutating verb is registered on `/settings` at all.** Not a route that refuses — no route. The stylesheet and the dashboard's script are served from `self`, embedded in the binary via `go:embed`; a client-side library would be too, and never from a CDN. If a change needs `unsafe-inline` to work, the change is wrong. `no-store` is the default rather than the exception, because a page, a stream, and an authorisation decision are all things a cached copy outlives: pages carry session names, working directories, and pane content, all secret under §3. **The two embedded static assets are the only exemption** — they hold no session data, and they are served `no-cache` with an entity tag rather than a lifetime, so a browser revalidates instead of running the previous binary's script against this one's markup. Every byte a milestone 1 client sees is frozen, and a header is part of a response. ### The header that must never appear | Header | Rule | |---|---| | `Access-Control-Allow-*` | **Never sent. Any of them, on any route, on either door.** | This is load-bearing, not hygiene. The browser's credential is a cookie and therefore **ambient**: it rides on requests a hostile third-party page triggers, and the edge converts those into a valid assertion the daemon accepts. Same-origin policy is the only thing stopping that page from *reading* the response, and it holds exactly as long as the daemon never opts out of it. An absent header is not evidence of same-origin initiation, and treating it as such makes the check optional for anything that can omit it. It is still only half the defence: the other half is the page token, because a header a future proxy could strip must not be the whole of it. ## Rendering session output (the one XSS surface) Everything a Claude session prints — file contents, command output, error text, a web page it fetched — reaches the dashboard. **All of it is untrusted.** ```go // html/template escapes by default. It is the only durable state the daemon keeps, and it exists because the host
stopped being sufficient: on 2026-08-22 the kernel OOM killer took a whole
`tmux-spawn` cgroup and destroyed a session's tmux state along with it, so
everything recorded on that tmux session went too.

**What it holds**: session id, owner, session name, conversation identifier,
working directory, start-command *name*, lifetime, original creation time, and a
revival attempt count. That is the set the daemon cannot rediscover once the
shell is gone. The session name is caller-supplied but not free text:
`ValidateName` holds it to `^[a-zA-Z0-9-]{1,64}$` before it is a session's, and a
revival cannot render its start command without it.

**What it must never hold**: a bearer token, a token hash, pane content,
conversation content, or caller-supplied free text. The rule FR-042 places on the
audit trail applies here unchanged — there is simply no request behind this file.
A start-command *name* is recorded and a command *line* never is: a stored
command line would be a command line a restart could be made to run.

**Mode `0600`**, created with the directory at `0700`.

**One journal per daemon, named after its listen address** — the same thing the
tmux server is named after (`tmuxctl.SocketFor`). Two daemons on one host must not
replay each other's sessions any more than they may see each other's shells, and
without this they do: a second daemon sharing a home directory replays the first
one's journal, finds those sessions absent from its *own* tmux server, and stands
ready to recreate every one of them on it.

**Append-only, fsynced per record.** The failure being defended against is an
unclean stop, and a rewritten document degrades to a truncated file where a log
degrades to a missing last line. On this host the unclean reset of 2026-08-17
lost a flag out of a rewritten `~/.claude.json` and took a gitignored `.env` with
it — that is the failure mode, observed, on this machine.

**Reading it is fail-loud, replaying it is fail-safe.** A missing file means no
session has been created yet. An unreadable one is fatal at startup, because a
daemon that continued would supervise nothing and report nothing. A torn final
line is discarded and counted. And every replayed candidate is re-checked against
the allowlist, the ceiling and the cap in force *now* — a journal outlives the
configuration that produced it, and it must never reinstate a session the
operator's current configuration would refuse to create.

## Claude Code's workspace trust (a file this daemon edits but does not own)

Before typing a start command, the daemon sets
`projects[].hasTrustDialogAccepted` to `true` in the `.claude.json` a
session will read (`$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, else `$HOME`, from the session's own
environment). Without it a session in a never-trusted directory sits on Claude
Code's trust dialog with nobody to answer it (`internal/session/trust.go`).

**This grants nothing `allowed_roots` did not.** Only a directory `ResolveWorkDir`
accepted reaches it, and a session there already runs with tool approval off.

**It edits someone else's file, so it touches as little as it can.** An
already-trusted directory is read and not rewritten. A missing file stays
missing. A rewrite takes the `.lock` flock ai-lawnmower's `trust-seed.sh`
takes, carries every other value through as raw JSON, and replaces the file by
rename. A file that is not a JSON object fails the create rather than being
repaired. Wired only in `httpapi.New`, so no test server reaches the operator's
real file. Not wired in kubernetes mode.

`trust_level = "trusted"` in `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml` (else `$HOME/.codex`), from the
session's own environment (`internal/session/trust_codex.go`). Everything above holds: it
grants nothing `allowed_roots` did not, an already-trusted directory is not rewritten, a
rewrite takes the `.lock` flock and replaces the file by rename, and it is wired only in
`httpapi.New`.

- **No TOML library.** The root module has no dependencies (section 5). The edit is line-level
  and understands exactly the shape Codex writes itself: that header line and a `trust_level`
  line in the table. Any other mention of the directory refuses the create rather than being
  edited.
- **A missing `config.toml` is created at 0600** when `$CODEX_HOME` exists, because Codex's own
  trust acceptance creates the same table in the same file. A missing `$CODEX_HOME` stays
  missing: Codex has never run there.
- **The trust level is never passed with `-c` on the command line.** That would put a
  caller-influenced path into a line typed at a shell, and no line this daemon types carries one.

### Codex conversation listing (amendment to spec 013 FR-025, spec 019 D11)

FR-025 says a transcript is never opened, because Claude's file name is the id and its
directory is the working directory. Codex keys rollouts by date and the working directory
exists only inside line 1, so listing a Codex directory's conversations opens each rollout
**once, bounded**: at most 64 KiB read, stopping at the first newline, decoding only `type`,
`payload.id` and `payload.cwd`. Nothing it reads is rendered or logged. It scans at most 500
rollout files, newest date directory first, and returns at most 50 matches. Claude's listing
still opens nothing.

### Codex's update check (spec 019 D5)

Codex checks for a new release on startup and offers to install it. A line typed into a pane
can answer that offer, so an update prompt is a way for typed input to install software. The
daemon therefore adds `-c check_for_update_on_startup=false` to every Codex line it types
(and `--no-alt-screen`, without which tmux keeps no scrollback), and configuration refuses a
Codex command that sets the check back to true. It is a daemon-owned flag, not an operator
choice, because a forgotten flag costs a global package install.

### Codex's dangerous flags are the operator's

`--dangerously-skip-permissions` is the operator's choice for Claude Code, and for Codex the
equivalents are `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` (no approval prompts, no sandbox)
and `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` (hooks run without review). The daemon adds neither.
Put them in the `codex` entry of `start_commands` if you want unattended sessions, with the
same consequences as for Claude: a request that passes auth runs code on this host unsandboxed.

## Rate limiting & audit

- Per-caller rate limit on session creation. Spawning Claude sessions is expensive
  and unbounded spawning is a local denial of service. **Both doors create**, so the
  browser's create calls the same limiter and the same validation rather than a second
  copy of either.
- Per-source rate limit on `POST /login`, on **the same token bucket**, which is generic
  over its key rather than duplicated: a create's budget is spent by an identity because
  it sits behind layer 2, and a sign-in's is spent by an address because establishing an
  identity is what it is for. The type parameter is what keeps one from being spent by
  the other's key. Two limiters over two copies of the bucket would be two rules about
  what a budget is, free to disagree.
- **What that limiter remembers is bounded by its own sweep**, and since the sign-in
  budget exists that is load-bearing: its keys are addresses a stranger chooses, so what
  keeps the map small is that every decision drops every bucket that has refilled to the
  top — an entry survives only while it is partly spent.
- Cap concurrent sessions; refuse past the cap rather than degrading the host.
- **Every request is audited**: timestamp, caller ID, action, session ID, decision.
  Audit records carry no prompt text and no session output.
- A browser action is audited under its own name — `dashboard.create`,
  `dashboard.destroy`, `dashboard.rename`, `dashboard.compact` — and a request the
  action gate refused under `dashboard.reject`, deliberately not `access.reject`: an
  identity that got in and *then* failed the cross-site check is a different and more
  alarming event than one that never got in, and an operator counting one must not be
  counting the other with it.
- **What was delivered is never recorded.** The compact's own text is a constant the
  daemon sends into a session; the record says the action happened, never its content.
  Every reason on the trail is a sentinel this codebase authored, so a record can
  never carry a byte the caller chose.

## Pre-merge security checklist

- [ ] No secret added to the repo (CI + push protection verify this)
- [ ] Every new endpoint enforces authn **and** ownership server-side
- [ ] Session IDs unguessable; a session another caller owns, or one that never
      existed, returns 404 and not 403 — the 403 is the action gate's answer to a
      request it would not accept at all, and the two never stand in for each other
- [ ] Any new mutating browser route goes through the action gate, not just layer 1,
      and both halves of that gate are tested with the other satisfied
- [ ] Input decoded into a typed struct with unknown fields rejected
- [ ] No shell string built; `exec.Command` with argv only
- [ ] Any caller-supplied path allowlisted and symlink-resolved
- [ ] Auth failures are uniform and leak no detail about which check failed
- [ ] No session output, prompt, or token in any log line
- [ ] Listener still bound to loopback, or bound wider only on a daemon whose
      layer 1 admits somebody
- [ ] A new setting a secret could be written into is classified by `config.IsSecret`,
      so the 0600 refusal and the settings page cannot disagree about it
- [ ] No secret value on any rendered page — swept across every route, not reasoned about
- [ ] No new dependency without justification, and the root `go.sum` still absent
- [ ] No `Access-Control-Allow-*` on any route, either door — swept, not assumed
- [ ] Browser-door responses all carry the header set above, refusals included

Hardens `POST /sessions/{id}/prompt`, the route lawnmower's `answer` and opp-lease
handoff already use, so a voice `steer` could use it later. Source of the

Spec Kit lane: research, spec, plan and tasks are written and committed before any Go
changes. The spec lives at `specs/020-prompt-route-safety/` because 018 and 019 are
already taken here.

## Conventions

- `- [ ]` open, `- [x]` done, `- [!]` blocked (reason in PROGRESS.md).

  says how to prove it.

## Decisions already made (copy these into research.md; do not reopen them)

- **D1 Spec number.** `specs/020-prompt-route-safety`. 018 is interactive-input, 019 is codex-runtime.
- **D2 Liveness gate (req 1).** Probe check 13: `@crswd-binary` matched `pane_current_command`
  (`claude`) on 6 of 6 live panes, 3 of them `rcq`. The gate reads the session's row from the
  controller's `List` and its `Claude` liveness. `LivenessStopped` refuses. `LivenessUnknown`
  passes, as spec 012 FR-006 reads it. It runs before the paste and again after the paste; if
  the second read is stopped, the daemon sends `C-u` and no Enter. No new `Controller` method,
  so the k8s module's `podctl` is untouched.
- **D3 Not-ready answer (reqs 1, 2, 5).** One sentinel `session.ErrSessionNotReady`. The prompt
  handler maps it to `409` with body `{"error":"session not ready"}` and an audit Deny with reason
  `session not ready`. A `failed` session gets it. `dead` stays as it is today.
- **D4 Bracketed paste (req 3).** `Manager.Prompt` uses `PasteBracketed` for every harness.
  `Manager.Compact` keeps its harness-based paste. No newline refusal: the opp-lease handoff
  pastes multi-line item bodies.
- **D5 Leading `!` or `/` (req 4).** API door only. Refuse when the first character that is not
  space, tab, CR or LF is `!` or `/`: `400` with the uniform bad-request body, before any tmux
  command. Grep of 10/14/26: lawnmower's callers (`console.py` `_answer_action` via
  `session_resume.deliver`, `lawnmower-route` `resume_prompt`, `_batch_listing_prompt`,
  `opp_followup_prompt`) all start with a letter. The browser type route is unchanged. This
  amends spec 018 FR-006 ("the API door's prompt route MUST be unchanged").

121	  Release notes: https://github.com/openai/codex/releases/latest
122	› 1. Update now (runs `npm install -g @openai/codex`)
123	  2. Skip
124	  3. Skip until next version
125	  Press enter to continue
126	```

129	```

131	│ >_ OpenAI Codex (v0.153.4)                               │
132	│                                                          │
133	│ model:       gpt-5.6-sol   /model to change              │
134	│ directory:   /home/op/code/repo                          │
135	│ permissions: YOLO mode                                   │
136	╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

146	```

148	## D. Decisions
149	
150	Each decision names the rejected alternative and why.
151	
152	**D1. A harness is derived from the configured command, never stored.**
153	`harness.Of(command)` is the base name of the command's first token (`startBinary`'s rule,
154	`internal/session/conversation.go:362`): `claude` → Claude, `codex` → Codex, anything else →
155	Other. A session already persists its start-command *name* in `@crswd-start` and the journal's
156	`start` field, and adoption restores both; the harness is recomputed from the configured
157	command each time it is needed.
158	*Rejected: a stored `@crswd-runtime` option.* Spec 009's lesson is that a fact tmux does not
159	hold is lost on adoption. Storing a second copy of something derivable creates a fact that can
160	disagree with the configuration it came from. *Rejected: a `harness=` field in the
161	configuration.* It would let an operator label `claude` as Codex; the binary already says what it is.
162	
163	**D2. A create still carries a name, never a command line.** The operator configures Codex as
164	a named entry in `start_commands`, e.g.
165	`codex=/home/nctiggy/sf-cli/bin/codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust`.
166	The browser offers Codex only when an entry named exactly `codex` exists and `harness.Of` of its
167	command is Codex. The signed API can already name `codex` (`start_command`).
168	*Rejected: offering every configured name.* That is spec 011's "harness picker" in general form;
169	this spec ships the two runtimes Craig asked for and keeps the browser's allowlist two entries long.
170	
171	**D3. Mode (local/remote) stays Claude-only.** `ModeRemote` means `claude --remote-control`.
172	A Codex session is always `local`; the browser refuses `remote_control=on` with `harness=codex`.
173	*Rejected: generalising Mode into "which named command".* docs/harnesses.md asked; the answer is
174	that Mode and harness are different axes, and Codex has no remote mode to put on the second value.
175	
176	**D4. Remote control for Codex is a non-goal.** `codex remote-control` manages an app-server
177	daemon that the ChatGPT mobile app pairs with; it does not attach to a TUI running in tmux
178	(research-codex.md §1). Spec 018's typed input is how a Codex session is driven from a phone.
179	
180	**D5. Required flags are added by the daemon, not left to configuration.** Codex's harness spec
181	carries two flag groups that crswd inserts after the binary on every line it types, unless the
182	exact token sequence is already in the configured command:
183	- `--no-alt-screen`: without it Codex draws on the alternate screen and tmux keeps no history,
184	  which defeats spec 018's scrollback.
185	- `-c check_for_update_on_startup=false`: M12. Without it any typed input can install software.
186	The approval/sandbox and hook-trust flags stay the operator's choice, as
187	`--dangerously-skip-permissions` is for Claude. *Rejected: documenting the two flags and trusting
188	the operator.* M12 shows a forgotten flag costs a global package install; a daemon that types into
189	the pane has to own the flags that make typing safe.
190	
191	**D6. Liveness compares against a set of names.** `@crswd-binary` changes from one name to names
192	joined by `|` (each still `[A-Za-z0-9._-]`), and the tmux format becomes
193	`#{?#{@crswd-binary},#{m/r:^(#{@crswd-binary})$,#{pane_current_command}},?}` (M17). Codex writes
194	`codex|node`; every other harness writes `startBinary(template)` exactly as today, so a Claude
195	session's option value and liveness answer are unchanged.
196	*Rejected: walking `/proc` from the daemon on every sweep.* One tmux format is cheaper and is what
197	podctl already reuses through `tmuxctl.ArgvList`. *Rejected: requiring the operator to configure
198	the native binary path.* The npm path is what is installed; a session that reads as permanently
199	stopped would be revived in a loop.
200	*Accepted risk:* while Codex runs, any `node` in the pane foreground reads as alive. The pane runs
201	nothing but the configured command.
202	
203	**D7. Codex conversations are discovered from `/proc`, not guessed.** Codex cannot be given an id
204	(no `--session-id`; `ThreadStartParams` has no id field). M6 shows the native process holds its
205	rollout open, so on each supervisor sweep a running Codex session with no conversation reads
206	`#{pane_pid}`, walks its descendants through `/proc/<pid>/task/<pid>/children` (depth ≤ 6, ≤ 64
207	processes), and reads each `/proc/<pid>/fd/*` link. A link matching
208	`<codexHome>/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-*-<uuid>.jsonl` yields the id.
209	*Rejected: matching rollouts by `cwd` and start time.* Two Codex sessions in one directory make it
210	a guess, and a wrong guess resumes someone else's conversation.
211	*Before the first prompt there is no id.* The session is supervised but not revivable by id, which
212	is exactly how a Claude session created before spec 012 behaves (`reasonNoConversation`). The card
213	says "conversation not yet started".
214	
215	**D8. Restarting a Codex session uses a stepped, verified quit.** Continue (spec 013) and revival
216	type a new command line into the pane. Into a live Codex composer that line becomes a prompt. So
217	for Codex `restartInto` sends one `C-c`, waits 1.5 s, asks tmux whether the pane is still running
218	the harness (D6), and repeats, at most 5 presses (M9 converged in 3). If the pane is still running
219	Codex after the fifth, it returns `ErrQuitUnconfirmed` and types nothing. Claude keeps `C-c C-c`.
220	*Rejected: `/quit` via paste.* While a turn runs, Codex queues typed input, so `/quit` would wait.
221	
222	**D9. Prompt and compact use bracketed paste on Codex (M3, M4, M5).**
223	Spec 018 adds `Controller.PasteBracketed` (`paste-buffer -p`). Claude keeps `Paste`; spec 018 owns
224	whether Claude moves to bracketed paste too.
225	
226	**D10. Codex trust is seeded by a line-level edit of `config.toml`.** No TOML library: the root
227	module has no dependencies (docs/security.md §5). The edit understands exactly one shape, the one
228	Codex itself writes (M2 and research-codex.md §5): a header line `[projects."<dir>"]` and a
229	`trust_level = "<value>"` line in that table. Anything else that mentions the directory refuses
230	rather than edits. Same lock file convention and atomic replace as `trust.go` (`<file>.lock`,
231	temp file, rename). A missing `config.toml` is created at 0600 when `$CODEX_HOME` exists, because
232	Codex's own trust acceptance creates the same table in the same file; a missing `$CODEX_HOME`
233	is left missing (Codex has never run, and will show sign-in first).
234	*Rejected: `-c 'projects."<dir>".trust_level="trusted"'` on the command line.* It puts a
235	caller-influenced path into a line typed at a shell. No line crswd types has ever carried a path.
236	
237	**D11. Codex conversation listing opens the first line of a rollout, bounded.** Spec 013 FR-025
238	says no transcript is opened, because Claude's file name is the id and its directory is the cwd.
239	Codex keys rollouts by date, and the cwd exists only inside line 1. The reader opens a rollout,
240	reads at most 64 KiB, stops at the first newline, and decodes only `type`, `payload.id` and
241	`payload.cwd`. Nothing it reads is rendered. It scans at most 500 rollout files, newest date
242	directory first, and returns at most 50 matches. docs/security.md records this amendment.
243	
244	**D12. Sign-in for Codex is a device-code relay with no paste-back.** `codex login --device-auth`
245	prints a link and a code (F2); the operator enters the code in a browser and the CLI polls. So the
246	Codex relay shows the link and the code and has no code form; `Deliver` refuses with
247	`ErrNoCodeToDeliver`. Status comes from `codex login status`'s exit code (M14): 0 signed in;
248	1 with `Not logged in` on stdout signed out; anything else unknown.
249	*Rejected: `codex login` (browser).* It opens a localhost callback a phone cannot reach.
250	
251	**D13. One relay, one auth cache, one pill per harness that is configured.** The single
252	`Server.signin` becomes a map keyed by `harness.Name`, built for Claude when the default command is
253	Claude (unchanged) and for Codex when an entry named `codex` exists. `GET /dashboard/auth` keeps
254	its wire shape and gains `?harness=codex`; absent means Claude, so the existing client is unchanged.
255	The create gate asks the relay of the harness the create resolves to.
256	
257	**D14. Codex quota reads the `codex` provider's `weekly` window (M18).** The reader becomes
258	`ReadProvider(path, provider, window)`. When the cache has no `codex` provider or no window
259	the Codex meter is hidden (NC-1, Craig 2026-10-06), which is what this host will show today. The quota-axi `auth_required`
260	cause is investigated by one spike task (T034) and changes no crswd code.
261	
262	**D15. Kubernetes mode for Codex is gated on spec 017 and on one measurement.** Operator-run
263	measurement O-1 (tasks.md) measures whether Codex runs a turn with `auth.json` delivered the way spec
264	017 FR-015 delivers Claude's credential. It needs a cluster and a real credential, so it is not a
265	loop task. Phase 4's credential tasks are planned from that measurement
266	in a follow-up planning pass; this spec does not guess them. The tasks that do not depend on it
267	(env pass-through, the in-pod conversation lookup, the session image) are written here.
268	
269	## Not verified
270	
271	- How an expired Codex login looks mid-session (needs a real expiry).
272	- The rendered text of Codex's usage-limit message (binary strings only: `hit your usage limit`).
273	- Whether a trusted parent directory covers a child in Codex.
274	- Whether `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` still shows the hooks dialog on any version.
275	- Whether Codex tolerates a read-only or access-token-only `auth.json` (O-1).
276	
277	## Critic findings (Codex critic pass, 10/6/26)
278	
279	Two `codex exec` critic passes (one aimed at spec 018, which also reviewed 019) returned 50 items;
280	32 concerned this spec. After dedupe, 29 were verified against the code and folded into tasks.md:
281	
282	| Finding | Fixed in |
283	|---|---|
284	| `[!]` tasks are skipped: `ralph/loop.sh` stops only on a non-zero iteration exit, and an iteration that marks `[!]` exits 0 | every codex-* `PROMPT.md` "Blocked" rule |
285	| Operator `-c check_for_update_on_startup=true` overrides the daemon's `false`; tokens after `--` treated as flags | T004a, T004 |
286	| Failed stepped quit after `Continue` persisted (`manager.go:2492-2506`) | T009 |
287	| `containedIn` (`conversation.go:249`) is lexical; symlinked rollouts | T010a `codexRollout` |
288	| Discovery write order not retry-safe | T012 (option → journal → store) |
289	| T014 / T022 / T013 / T003 Files lines missing files they edit | T014, T022a–c, T013, T003 + allowlists |
290	| No header model: templates pass `.Operator` | T025 `headerView` |
291	| `binaryOf` drops an absolute path | T021 `executable` |
292	| T040 needs a cluster and credentials; no cleanup | O-1 (operator-run) |
293	| `/proc` walk unbounded per process | T011 caps + `ErrDiscoveryBounds` |
294	| T010, T022 too big | T010a/b, T022a/b/c |
295	| Multi-pill script races; meter/label pairing | T025, T032 |
296	| T041 blocked by T040 against D15 | T041 |
297	| In-pod `CODEX_HOME` default | T042 |
298	| Other renders "Other" | T016 |
299	| No radio component exists | T014a |
300	| Update-check placement for `login` unmeasured | T021 uses top-level `-c` |
301	| T021 anchor in wrong package | T021 |
302	| testdata README absent | T013 |
303	| Harness value multiplicity | T014 `parseHarness`, used by T016, T022b, T024, T031 |
304	| `Other` routed to Claude conversation lookups | T010b exhaustive dispatch |
305	| `Type` would lose bracketed paste for Claude | T005 guardrail |
306	| `cardOf` has no receiver | T013 parameter |
307	| Codex panel forms default to the Claude relay | T024 hidden field |
308	| Redirect cannot reopen the Codex dialog | T024 `signin=codex`, T025 |
309	| No 409 path in sign-in | T024 keeps the 303 refused outcome |
310	| CRLF and duplicate headers in `config.toml` | T007 |
311	| T034 cannot run first under topmost-open | T034 moved above T030 |
312

314	
315	- **R-1. M17 stores escaped bars.** Rejected: `\|` in M17 is Markdown table escaping. The bytes
316	  set with `tmux set-option` and stored in `@crswd-binary` are `codex|node|sleep`, raw, and T002's

# Research: Codex as a first-class runtime

**Spec**: [spec.md](spec.md) · **Plan**: [plan.md](plan.md) · **Tasks**: [tasks.md](tasks.md)

Everything below marked Measured was run on `claude-server` on 10/6/26 against
`codex-cli 0.153.4` (`/home/nctiggy/sf-cli/bin/codex`) and tmux 3.4, in a private tmux
server (`tmux -L <name>`) with an isolated `CODEX_HOME`, so the operator's
`~/.codex/config.toml` was not touched. Anything not measured says so.

## M. Measurements

| # | Question | Measured answer |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | What does tmux report as `#{pane_current_command}` while Codex runs? | `node`. `~/sf-cli/bin/codex` is a symlink to `@openai/codex/bin/codex.js`, a Node wrapper that spawns the native binary `…/codex-linux-x64/vendor/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/bin/codex`. After Codex exits the pane reports `bash`. |
| M2 | Does a pre-written `[projects."<dir>"] trust_level = "trusted"` in `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml` suppress the trust prompt? | Yes. With the table written before start, Codex went straight to the composer. |
| M3 | Does crswd's prompt delivery (`load-buffer`, `paste-buffer -d`, then `send-keys Enter`) submit on Codex? | **No.** The text lands in the composer and the Enter is swallowed. A second Enter sent ~12 s later submitted it. |
| M4 | Does bracketed paste (`paste-buffer -p -d`) followed by `send-keys Enter` submit? | **Yes**, for one line and for a two-line paste. Both turns completed. |
| M5 | Does `/compact` delivered as bracketed paste + Enter work? | Yes. The pane printed `• Context compacted`. |
| M6 | Where is the conversation id before and after the first prompt? | No rollout file exists until the first prompt. After it, the native `codex` process holds the rollout **open**: `/proc/<native pid>/fd/37 -> $CODEX_HOME/sessions/2026/10/06/rollout-2026-10-06T00-11-13-01a10e8c-d5f5-7452-8561-233103b38287.jsonl`, still open while idle after the turn. |
| M7 | Process tree under the pane | `pane_pid` (bash) → `node …/bin/codex` → native `codex`. `/proc/<pid>/task/<pid>/children` lists children on this kernel. |
| M8 | What does Ctrl-C do? | Idle with an empty composer: one `C-c` exits to the shell and prints `To continue this session, run: codex resume <id>`. During a turn: `C-c C-c` interrupts (`■ Conversation interrupted …`) and **does not exit**. Esc then `C-c C-c` one second later also did not exit. |
| M9 | Does a stepped quit converge? | Yes. During a turn with half-typed text in the composer: `C-c`, wait 1.5 s, check `pane_current_command`; repeated, the pane was back at `bash` after the **third** press. |
| M10 | Does `codex resume <id> <flags…>` accept the top-level flags after the subcommand? | Yes. `codex resume <id> --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox --no-alt-screen --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust -c check_for_update_on_startup=false` restored the conversation (history visible, `Context compacted` line included). |
| M11 | `codex resume <id that does not exist>` | Prints `ERROR: No saved session found with ID <id>. Run codex resume without an ID to choose from existing sessions.` and exits to the shell. **No picker.** |
| M12 | Is the update prompt dangerous? | **Yes. This is the most important finding.** On `codex resume`, Codex 0.153.4 drew a blocking menu: `✨ Update available! 0.153.4 -> 0.160.1` / `› 1. Update now (runs npm install -g @openai/codex)` / `2. Skip` / `3. Skip until next version` / `Press enter to continue`. A prompt delivered blind (paste + Enter) selected item 1 and started a global `npm install -g @openai/codex`. It was interrupted by the next Ctrl-C; npm rolled back (verified: `codex --version` still 0.153.4, files still dated 9/8). |
| M13 | Can the update check be turned off per launch? | Yes. `-c check_for_update_on_startup=false` on the command line suppressed the menu on the same `resume` that showed it before. The key is in the binary's config schema. |
| M14 | `codex login status` exit codes | Signed in: prints `Logged in using ChatGPT`, exit 0. Empty `CODEX_HOME`: prints `Not logged in` on **stderr** (stdout is empty), exit 1. Read both streams. |
| M15 | `codex login --device-auth` screen (CLI, not the TUI) | Captured below (§F2). The code is two upper-case alphanumeric groups joined by `-`. |
| M16 | `session_meta` first line of a rollout | JSON object `{"timestamp","ordinal","type":"session_meta","payload":{…}}`; payload keys include `id`, `session_id`, `cwd`, `originator` (`codex-tui`), `cli_version`, `timestamp`, `base_instructions`. Line length on this host: 18–23 KB (62 rollouts, max 22,455 bytes) because `base_instructions` is inline. |
| M17 | tmux regex format match | `#{m/r:^(#{@crswd-binary})$,#{pane_current_command}}` with `@crswd-binary` = `codex\|node\|sleep` (raw bytes `codex|node|sleep`; the backslashes are table escaping) returned `1` for a pane running `sleep`, and `0` with `codex\|node`. tmux 3.4 here; the session image ships 3.5a. |
| M18 | quota-axi `codex` provider | `providers/codex.js:134` names the windows `five_hour` and `weekly`. The cache file on this host (`~/.cache/quota-axi/quotas.json`) holds only the `claude` provider. `quota-axi --provider codex --full` reports `auth_required` although `codex login status` says signed in; this account is Business with unlimited credits, and `account/rateLimits/read` returns `primary: null, secondary: null`. Cause of `auth_required`: **not measured**. |
| M19 | Why does quota-axi report `auth_required` for Codex? | Measured 2026-10-06 by the operator session (quota-axi as installed, Codex 0.153.4). `quota-axi auth` lists `~/.codex/auth.json` and the cli-rpc binary as `available`; the access token is valid (not expired). `quota-axi --provider codex --full`: oauth `failed` "Codex sign-in required", cli-rpc `failed` "Codex quota unavailable". Cause: an unlimited Business account has no windows and quota-axi mislabels that as `auth_required`. **Fix belongs to quota-axi** (report `unlimited`/no-windows from a 200 with `credits.unlimited`). No crswd change: the Codex meter stays hidden while no window exists (NC-1). |
| M20 | Session image carries `codex` | Measured 10/6/26 on the published `ghcr.io/craig-ai-tooling/crswd-session:2.0.161`, in a live session pod on lm-amd64-1: `command -v codex` printed `/usr/local/bin/codex`, `codex --version` printed `codex-cli 0.153.4`, and `claude --version` printed `2.1.246 (Claude Code)`. A Codex session started from the chart drew Codex's sign-in screen, as expected for a namespace with no `codex-auth` Secret. |

Exit **0**. First try on `node:22-slim` exited 1 with `Failed to load cloud config bundle (workspace-managed policies)`: that image has no CA bundle. |
| M22 | `auth.json` mtime across a turn after access-token expiry | **Not measured: token not expired** (237.9 h left on 10/6/26, `last_refresh` the same day). |
| M23 | A Codex turn with the Secret mounted read-only at `$CODEX_HOME/auth.json` (subPath, no copy) | Exit **0**, same run as M21. Host `~/.codex/auth.json` mtime unchanged after both pods and `codex login status` still `Logged in using ChatGPT`. # Research: prompt route safety

**Spec**: [spec.md](spec.md) · **Plan**: [plan.md](plan.md) · **Tasks**: [tasks.md](tasks.md)

The requirements come from `~/code/ai-lawnmower/docs/mcp-session-steering-design.md`,
section (g) "Phase 3 detail", and the evidence from the probe run recorded in
`~/code/ai-lawnmower/ralph/plans/lm-steer-design/results.md`. Both live outside this
repository and are read, never edited. Everything cited below as a *probe check* is a
numbered check in that results file; everything cited as *measured here* was read off
this tree on 10/14/26 and is restated in `ralph/plans/lm-steer-crswd-018/PROGRESS.md`
so a later iteration need not re-measure it.

The decisions were taken before the plan was cut. They are recorded here in full so the
spec, the plan and the task list all cite one source. **They are not reopened by this
spec** — a decision that needs changing needs a new one, with its own evidence.

## D1 — Spec number

The spec lives at `specs/020-prompt-route-safety/`.

The design calls this work "crswd spec 018". That number is taken here: `specs/018-interactive-input`
is the session page's input panel and `specs/019-codex-runtime` is the Codex runtime
(measured here: both directories exist and carry a `spec.md`). The next free number is 020.

*Rejected: reusing 018 because the design names it.* A spec directory is addressed by
number from `tasks.md`, from `docs/`, and from the two specs that this one amends; two
specs under one number is a reference that resolves to the wrong document.

## D2 — Liveness gate (requirement 1)

`Manager.Prompt` reads the session's row out of the controller's `List` and consults its
`Claude` liveness before it pastes, and again after the paste:

- `LivenessStopped` returns `ErrSessionNotReady` and nothing is typed.
- `LivenessUnknown` delivers, which is how spec 012 FR-006 reads that value — an
  unknown liveness is not evidence of a stopped harness.
- A failing `List` is an error, not a pass. The gate fails closed.
- If the *second* read is stopped — Claude exited between the paste and the submit — the
  daemon sends `C-u` and no Enter, so the half-delivered text is cleared off the shell's
  line rather than executed by it, and the call still answers `ErrSessionNotReady`.

Evidence: probe check 13 — the `@crswd-binary` tmux option matched `pane_current_command`
(`claude`) on 6 of 6 live panes, 3 of them under `rcq`. So the option this daemon already
sets is a usable liveness answer on the panes lawnmower actually drives, and the gate
needs no new fact on the host.

Measured here: the fake controller's `List` already derives `Claude` liveness from
`@crswd-binary` against the pane command (`livenessOf`), and the fake has
`SetPaneCommand(name, command)` to drive it.

*Rejected: a per-session liveness method on `tmuxctl.Controller`.* There is none today,
and the interface has a second implementation — `k8s/internal/podctl` — which a seventh
method would force to change. `k8s/` is out of this milestone's reach by construction, so
the gate reads the row it can already get.

*Rejected: trusting the stored session state alone.* A pane whose harness exited is still
`running` in the store until the next supervisor sweep; the whole point of the gate is to
answer for the pane as it is at the moment of the paste.

## D3 — Not-ready answer (requirements 1, 2, 5)

One sentinel, `session.ErrSessionNotReady`, carries every "the session cannot take a
prompt right now" refusal. The prompt handler maps it to `409` with body
`{"error":"session not ready"}` and records an audit Deny whose reason is the sentinel's
text, `session not ready`.

A session in state `failed` is refused with it before any tmux command runs. `dead` keeps
the answer it gives today (`ErrSessionDead`), because that is a frozen client-visible
behaviour and nothing in this spec asks to change it.

Evidence: lawnmower's `deliver()` (`~/code/ai-lawnmower/loop/session_resume.py`) already
treats any response body carrying an `error` key as a refusal, so a 409 of this shape
reads as a refusal to the only caller this route has today without a change on that side.

One sentinel rather than three keeps the refusal uniform: the caller learns that the
session is not ready and not *which* of the gates said so. The three are distinguished
only server-side, on the trail.

## D4 — Bracketed paste (requirement 3)

`Manager.Prompt` pastes with `PasteBracketed` for every harness. `Manager.Compact` keeps
its harness-based paste and is untouched.

Evidence: spec 019 M3/M4 measured that a plain `paste-buffer -d` plus Enter does not
submit on Codex while `paste-buffer -p -d` plus Enter does, for one line and for two;
spec 018 added `Controller.PasteBracketed` and left "whether Claude moves to bracketed
paste too" to be decided. This is that decision, and it is taken for both harnesses so
that one route has one delivery shape. Bracketed paste is also what makes the C0 refusal
in `docs/security.md` §2 load-bearing rather than decorative: inside a bracketed paste a
literal `ESC[201~` would end the paste, and that text is already refused.

**No newline refusal.** The opp-lease handoff pastes multi-line item bodies (the fixtures
in `ralph/plans/lm-steer-crswd-018/PROGRESS.md` are multi-line as lawnmower builds them
today), so refusing `\n` would refuse the traffic this route exists to carry.

Measured here: `m.paste` is bracketed only when the harness spec says `BracketedPaste`,
which Claude's does not — so this is a behaviour change for Claude sessions and needs the
failing-before test that proves it.

## D5 — A leading `!` or `/` is refused (requirement 4)

On the **API door only**, a prompt is refused when the first character that is not a
space, a tab, a CR or an LF is `!` or `/`: `400` with the uniform bad-request body,
before any tmux command runs.

`/` opens a Claude Code slash command and `!` opens its shell escape. A caller that can
reach this route can already run code on the host through a session, so this is not a
containment boundary; it is a refusal of the two prefixes that make a *delivered prompt*
mean something other than a prompt — a steering message that silently became `/clear` is
a lost conversation with no error anywhere.

Evidence: a grep of lawnmower's callers on 10/14/26 — `console.py` `_answer_action` (via
`session_resume.deliver`), `lawnmower-route` `resume_prompt`, `_batch_listing_prompt` and
`opp_followup_prompt` — found that every builder's text starts with a letter. A *later*
line starting with `/` does occur (the `resume.txt` fixture has one), which is why the
rule reads only the first non-whitespace character of the whole text and never a line.

**The browser type route is unchanged.** The operator typing into the session page's input
panel is a human at their own keyboard who may legitimately want `/compact`; spec 018 FR-006
says the API door's prompt route is unchanged, and this decision **amends that FR** for this
one refusal. The amendment is recorded in spec.md.

## D6 — The lock and the buffer (requirement 5)

`Prompt` takes the restart claim (`claimRestart`, non-blocking) immediately after
`lockSession`, refuses with `ErrSessionNotReady` when a revive or a continue already holds
it, and releases it on return.

Measured here, and therefore *not* new work in this spec:

- `lockSession` (`internal/session/input.go`) is already the per-session mutex shared by
  `Type`, `PressKey`, `Prompt`, `Compact`, `SetMode`, `Continue`, `Destroy` and the
  supervisor's Codex discovery. Two concurrent prompts to one session already serialise.
- `Exec.paste` (`internal/tmuxctl/exec.go`) already makes a fresh buffer name per paste
  via `newBufferName`, so two pastes cannot clobber one buffer. The fake records the
  names it was given (`nextBuffer`), so a test can assert they differ.

Both came out of the spec 018 and 019 reviews. What is new here is only the claim: a
revive or a continue is *typing a command line into the pane*, and a prompt pasted into
the middle of that line is neither a prompt nor a command. The claim is non-blocking on
purpose — a prompt that waited for a restart would be delivered into a session whose
conversation has since been replaced, which is worse than a refusal the caller can retry.

## D7 — `request_id` (requirement 6)

The prompt body gains one optional field, `request_id`: 1 to 32 characters of `[a-z0-9-]`.
A value outside that is `400`. A valid value is echoed in the `202` body and written as
`request_id` on the audit record. Absent means the field appears nowhere — not in the
response, not on the trail.

This **amends spec 001 FR-042** ("audit records carry no caller-supplied free text") for
this one field, and the bound is what makes the amendment safe to take: 32 characters of
`[a-z0-9-]` cannot carry prompt text, a sentence, a path, or a credential, and the
character class keeps it out of trouble in a JSONL record and in a log line. The
amendment is recorded in spec.md and in `specs/001-crswd-daemon-core/contracts/http-api.md`.

What it buys: lawnmower delivers a prompt and then reads the trail to find out what
happened to it. Without a correlator it matches on session ID and time, which is ambiguous
for exactly the case that matters — two deliveries to one session in one second.

**No length and no hash of the prompt**, here or anywhere else. The rule in
`docs/security.md` §3 stands unchanged: a length is a disclosure and a hash is a
disclosure of a guessable value.

## D8 — The registry gate (requirement 7) is deferred

Requirement 7 — consult Claude Code's `~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json` registry to decide
whether a session is ready — is **not built**, and the spec lists it under Out of scope
with this reason. It was a MAY in the design, not a MUST.

Evidence, all from the probe:

- Check 8 left open whether crswd can read `sessions/<pid>.json` at all under v2
  option B. No FR in spec 017 places that file in the cluster deployment, so a gate
  reading it would work on the VM and silently answer nothing in Kubernetes.
- Checks 3 and 9: the registry misses the trust dialog and misses a half-typed draft.
  So it does not answer the question the liveness gate (D2) answers, and a gate built on
  it would pass a session that cannot take a prompt.

A deferred MAY with a recorded reason is not an open question: **this is not a
NEEDS CLARIFICATION**, and nothing downstream waits on it.

## D9 — Out of scope

Named here so that a later iteration does not read one of these as missing work:

- **Opening a transcript.** Spec 013 FR-025 holds; the Codex exception (spec 019 D11) is
  that spec's and is not widened here.
- **Holding or calling an LLM.** This daemon delivers text; it does not author it.
- **A seventh API route.** The API door has six (measured here: the route switch in
  `internal/httpapi/server.go`, and six `## <VERB> <path>` headings in the contract).
  Every change in this spec lands on the existing prompt route.
- **Free text on the browser door beyond spec 018.** The session page's input panel is
  that spec's and keeps its behaviour, D5 included.
- **The startup lost-Enter window.** Probe check 1 found no check-then-Enter race after
  the first turn, and a lost Enter only inside roughly the first 5 s after a launch. That
  window is real and is not closed here.
- **The socket transport.** The probe's verdict was "flip to socket"; it binds the
  lm-steer-write milestone, not this one.
- **A new package under `internal/`.** Every change lands in `audit`, `httpapi`,
  `session` or `tmuxctl`.

## Not verified

- Whether Claude Code's registry file is reachable from a session pod (probe check 8,
  deferred with requirement 7 under D8).
- The exact width of the startup window in which an Enter can be lost; probe check 1
  bounds it at roughly 5 s and this spec does not depend on the number.
- Whether a `LivenessUnknown` pane can be running a harness that would swallow a paste.
  D2 delivers on unknown by spec 012 FR-006; no probe check contradicts it.
